thread.title: Tesla Has Rivals on Its Tail but That May Not Matter

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Tesla Has Rivals on Its Tail but That May Not Matter
text:
Illustration: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images By Teresa Rivas Sept. 17, 2018 1:08 p.m. ET Tesla shares are higher today, as at least one analyst thinks that the threat of competition has been overblown.
Where we were: Putting aside the erratic behavior of CEO Elon Musk , one of bears’ favorite fundamental arguments is that Tesla is facing a wave of rivals.
Where we’re headed: Yet Bernstein argues that major competitors won’t hit the market until at least 2020, and Tesla should have the brand power to fend them off.
Another day, another round of Tesla (TSLA) scrutiny.
Today, we got news that rival Lucid Motors inked a $1 billion investment agreement with Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund ; the nation was most recently in the auto spotlight thanks to Tesla’s potential go-private deal . Lucid said that the funding would allow it to launch its first electric vehicle, the Lucid Air, in 2020. In addition, Reuters reports that Volkswagen (VLKAF) plans to produce some 10 million electric cars.
Worries about CEO Elon Musk aside, one of the major components of the bear argument against the stock is growing competition , from both traditional auto makers and other upstarts. Yet when the rubber hits the road, that threat doesn’t look very worrisome, argues Bernstein’s Toni Sacconaghi.
Saccanaghi is no Tesla bull. He reiterated a Market Perform rating on the shares Monday, and Musk famously dismissed his question as boring during the company’s infamous first-quarter earnings call. Yet he writes that it’s clear that “there is no actual flood of competition coming.”
He counted every electric vehicle that’s expected to arrive in the U.S. between now and 2022, and writes that the results were “stark,” with Tesla’s Model 3, expected to represent as much as 70% of the company’s sales within two years, “faces no credible competition whatsoever until 2020,” until the arrival of Volvo’s Polestar 2. He also sees the Models S and X facing just two competitors until 2020 in the Audi E-tron Quattro and the Jaguar I-Pace.
In addition, the new electric offerings from conventional auto makers will likely help to validate and expand the market for electric vehicles overall. He likens it to the digital camera market in the early 2000s, or the flash-storage market today: Yes, incumbents took a majority share, but those markets grew so quickly that new entrants were still able to see plenty of growth.
“We also believe that the current hand-wringing over competition glosses over Tesla’s greatest long-term competitive advantage: its unparalleled brand,” he writes. Even when real competition does start to come on the scene, Saccanaghi writes that Tesla will likely be well positioned to defend its market share, much in the way that Apple (AAPL) has been able to perch atop the cutthroat smartphone market.
So why not a Buy rating? Well, just because external threats aren’t an issue yet, doesn’t mean that internal ones have gone. Saccanaghi writes that Tesla is its own worst enemy and execution remains the big question mark: Whether or not the company can build the Model 3 well and profitably.
Tesla is up 0.8% to $297.64 this afternoon.
